Question_text: A student investigates how a magnetic force varies with distance. A bar magnet is attracted to the iron base of a clamp stand, as shown in Fig. 1.1. A newton meter is attached to the magnet. The student pulls the newton meter vertically upwards and measures the force F required to pull the magnet off the iron base.
image: Fig. 1.1 shows a diagram of the experimental setup. A clamp stand with an iron base is depicted. A bar magnet rests on the iron base, attached by a string to a newton meter held vertically above it. A piece of tape is shown around the magnet. Labels include 'newton meter', 'string', 'tape', 'magnet', and 'iron base'.

Parts.part_text: Explain why it is difficult to measure F accurately.
Describe a method the student can use to measure F more accurately.
Fig. 1.2 shows the maximum reading on the newton meter as the magnet is pulled off the base. Record the force F shown on the newton meter.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.2 displays a close-up of a newton meter scale, calibrated in Newtons (N) from 0 to 10. The pointer indicates a reading of 6.6 N, positioned between the 6 N and 7 N marks.

Parts.part_text: The student places one sheet of paper between the magnet and the iron base and measures the force F to pull the magnet off the base. He repeats the experiment, each time increasing the number n of sheets of paper. The results obtained are recorded in Fig. 1.3. On Fig. 1.3, add your value for F from (b).
Parts.image: Fig. 1.3 is a table titled 'n' and 'F/N'. It shows data for the number of sheets of paper (n) and the corresponding force (F/N). The table includes rows for n=1, F=3.5; n=2, F=2.5; n=3, F=1.5; n=4, F=1.0; n=5, F=0.5. The entry for n=0 and F/N is left blank for the student to fill in.

Parts.part_text: On Fig. 1.4, plot a graph of F/N on the y-axis against n on the x-axis. Start your axes from the origin. Draw a smooth curve of best fit.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.4 is a blank grid for plotting a graph, with both the x-axis and y-axis originating from (0,0).

Parts.part_text: Describe how F varies with n.
The newton meter shown in Fig. 1.2 is not suitable for measuring F when there are more than 5 sheets of paper. Suggest why.
The student repeats the experiment using paper of a different thickness. His new value of F when n = 1 is 3.0N. State which paper is thicker. Give a reason for your answer.
Explain how using very thin paper improves the experiment.
Very thin sheets may be made from aluminium foil. State and explain whether aluminium foil is a suitable material for this experiment.

Question_text: A student investigates the reflection of light. The student has available: a pin board, a sheet of plain paper, a plane mirror, optical pins, a pencil, ruler and protractor.

Parts.part_text: Describe how the student uses the apparatus to verify that the angles of incidence and reflection are equal. Include a clear labelled diagram in your answer.
The student carries out the experiment carefully. Describe one practical technique that improves the accuracy of the experiment.

Question_text: A student uses a lemon to make a simple electric cell. He inserts a copper strip and an iron nail into the lemon, as shown in Fig. 3.1. The student connects a centre-zero voltmeter between the copper strip and the iron nail to measure the e.m.f. produced by the lemon cell.
image: Fig. 3.1 shows a diagram of a lemon with a copper strip and an iron nail inserted into it, forming a simple electric cell. The copper strip and iron nail are labelled.

Parts.part_text: Record the e.m.f. shown on the voltmeter.
Parts.image: Fig. 3.2 shows a centre-zero voltmeter scale. The scale ranges from -3 V to +3 V, marked with major divisions at 0, 1, 2, 3 and corresponding negative values. The pointer indicates a positive reading between 0 and 1, specifically at 0.9 V.

Parts.part_text: Suggest how the connecting leads from the voltmeter can be securely attached to the strip and to the nail.
State what happens if the connections to the voltmeter are reversed.
Suggest one reason why lemons are not used to power simple electronic equipment such as digital watches.
The student connects three lemon cells in series and measures the total e.m.f. with the voltmeter. State the total e.m.f. that you would expect.
On Fig. 3.3, draw the connections that the student uses.
Parts.image: Fig. 3.3 shows three schematic representations of lemon cells arranged vertically, one below the other. Each lemon has a copper strip and an iron nail inserted, serving as electrodes. Below the cells, a voltmeter symbol 'V' is shown. The task is to draw connections for a series circuit.

Parts.part_text: The student connects three lemon cells in parallel and measures the total e.m.f. with the voltmeter. State the total e.m.f. that you would expect.
On Fig. 3.4, draw the connections that the student uses.
Parts.image: Fig. 3.4 shows three schematic representations of lemon cells arranged vertically, one below the other. Each lemon has a copper strip and an iron nail inserted, serving as electrodes. Below the cells, a voltmeter symbol 'V' is shown. The task is to draw connections for a parallel circuit.

Question_text: A student is given a bag of ten similar marbles.

Parts.part_text: The student uses a 30 cm ruler to determine the average diameter of the marbles. Describe how the student obtains an accurate value. Include a labelled diagram showing how any additional apparatus is used.
The student then measures the diameter d of one marble accurately using a micrometer. The scale of the micrometer is shown in Fig. 4.1.
Parts.image: Fig. 4.1 shows a detailed diagram of a micrometer screw gauge scale. The sleeve scale shows divisions up to 10 mm, with a half-millimeter mark visible after 10 mm. The thimble scale, numbered from 20 to 40, shows its edge aligned with the 36th division. The micrometer is labelled.

Parts.part_text: State the reading shown on the micrometer.
Describe how the student checks that the marble is spherical.
